# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>

MANUFACTURERS' SHIPMENTS, INVENTORIES, & ORDERS

About the Surveys

PURPOSE

The purpose of the Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3) survey is to provide broad-based monthly statistical data on current economic conditions and indications of future production commitments in the manufacturing sector.

COVERAGE

The M3 is based upon data reported from manufacturing establishments with $500 million or more in annual shipments. Units may be divisions of diversified large companies, large homogenous companies, or single-unit manufacturers in 89 industry categories.

CONTENT

The M3 provides statistics on manufacturers' value of shipments, new orders (net of cancellations), end-of-month order backlog (unfilled orders), end-of-month total inventory, materials and supplies, work-in-process, and finished goods inventories (at current cost or market value). Data are collected and tabulated predominantly by 6-digit NAICS (North American Industry Classification System).

FREQUENCY

The survey has been conducted monthly by the US Census Bureau since 1957.

METHODS

Data are collected by FAX image capture (PFIRS) and Internet-based survey form (Census Taker). Data describe activities taking place during the calendar month.

PRODUCTS

There are two press releases per month. The first, Advance Report on Durable Goods Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders is available about 18 working days after each month. The second, Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders includes durable and non-durable manufacturing and is available about 23 working days after each month.

USES

Bureau of Economic Analysis uses M3 data to make GDP estimates and compiles the principal economic indicator series. The Federal Reserve Board, Department of Treasury, Council of Economic Advisers develop fiscal and monetary policy. Corporate economists, trade associations, news media, academia, investment consultants, and researchers use M3 data for analysis and forecasting of future economic conditions.

CONFIDENTIALITY

The U.S. Census Bureau is required by Section 9 of Title 13 United States Code to keep respondents' information confidential and can use the information only to produce statistics. The Census Bureau is not permitted to publicly release a respondent's information in a way that could identify a business, organization, or institution. Per the Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015, submitted data are protected from cybersecurity risks through screening of the systems that transmit the data.

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3)
Description: The Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3) survey provides broad-based, monthly statistical data on economic conditions in the domestic manufacturing sector. The survey measures current industrial activity and provides an indication of future business trends.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I checked the title and description you gave against the official Census Bureau M3 landing page. Both match the agency's own wording exactly. The research turned up a few points you may want to know about first:

- **No revisions for the rest of 2026.** Census says historical revisions and seasonal-adjustment model updates are paused for the remainder of 2026 because of "schedule and resource constraints."
- **The 2025 shutdown disrupted releases.** The October 2025 funding lapse delayed the advance and full reports.
- **The figures can't be tested for statistical significance.** The panel isn't a probability sample, so sampling error and confidence intervals can't be calculated.
- **Census's own pages contradict each other on some details.** They're listed in section 10.

---

# Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3) — Dataset Report

## 1. Checking your information

| Item | What you have | What I found |
|---|---|---|
| Title | Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3) | ✅ Correct. Also known as "Factory Orders," and the advance release is the "Durable Goods report." |
| Description | "provides broad-based, monthly statistical data on economic conditions in the domestic manufacturing sector… measures current industrial activity and provides an indication of future business trends." | ✅ Word for word what census.gov/manufacturing/m3 says. "Domestic" means the 50 states plus DC. |

## 2. Who publishes it

- **Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, part of the Department of Commerce. The survey is run by the Economic Indicators Division; the reporting address on the form is "EID/M3."
- **Status:** OMB designates it a **Principal Federal Economic Indicator (PFEI)**. That puts its release timing and handling under OMB statistical policy rules, including fixed release times and controls on access before release.
- **Contacts:** Census lists contact and respondent-help pages; the reporting site is econhelp.census.gov/m3, and burden comments go to eid.m3.qs@census.gov.

## 3. Legal authority and mandate

- **Authority to collect:** Title 13 U.S.C. §§ 131, 182, and 193, as cited on Form M-3(SD).
- **Response is voluntary.** That makes the program depend on companies' goodwill.
- **Confidentiality:** Title 13 § 9 lets Census use responses only for statistics and bars releasing anything that identifies a business. Data in transit are also protected under the Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act:** OMB control number **0607-0008**. Recent approval cycles include ICRs 202011-0607-004 and 202312-0607-002, and earlier approvals listed about 60,000 responses and 20,000 burden hours a year. Census estimates the form takes about 20 minutes. Check reginfo.gov for the current expiration date.
- **OMB's summary:** "This is the only survey that provides monthly statistical information… on the entire manufacturing sector," and it is "an essential part of the development of the Gross Domestic Product."

## 4. History

- **1939:** The Commerce Department's Office of Business Economics (OBE) starts the monthly "Industry Survey," published at first as indexes weighted by the Census of Manufactures.
- **1948–49:** OBE switches to dollar totals, begins seasonally adjusted figures, enlarges the panel, and benchmarks to IRS *Statistics of Income* data.
- **March 1957:** Collection and tabulation move to the Census Bureau. Census dates its monthly program from 1957.
- **Early 1960s:** A major revision covering 1947–1963 (led by Shirley Kallek, under Maxwell Conklin) adds more industry groups, benchmarks to the Annual Survey of Manufactures, introduces divisional reports for large companies, and adds market categories such as capital and consumer goods. Scans of these Current Industrial Reports are on archive.org.
- **1958–2001:** Historical series on the older SIC industry codes are still posted.
- **2001:** The survey converts to NAICS codes, with revised data back to January 1992. Census publishes crosswalk documents between the two systems.
- **2021:** Benchmarked to the 2017 Economic Census.
- **May 16, 2025:** The latest benchmark, to the 2022 Economic Census on a 2017 NAICS basis. It revised seasonally adjusted data from January 2012 and unadjusted data from January 2017.
- **July 25, 2025:** Starting with June 2025 data, the advance release adds detailed estimates for all nondurable industries (the "Advance Total Manufacturing" file).
- **October–November 2025:** The shutdown suspends releases. The October 2025 advance report came out December 23, 2025, and the full report January 7, 2026.
- **2026:** Revisions and seasonal-model updates are frozen for the rest of the year. The latest full report (August 2026 data) came out October 2, 2026; the September advance report is scheduled for October 27, 2026 and the full report for November 3, 2026.

## 5. What's in the data and how it's made

**Variables:** value of shipments; new orders (net of cancellations); unfilled orders (backlog); total inventories; inventories by stage (materials and supplies, work in process, finished goods); and inventory-to-shipment and unfilled-orders-to-shipment ratios. All are in current dollars and **not adjusted for inflation**.

**Panel design:**
- The universe is all manufacturing companies in the most recent Economic Census. In 2022 that was about 250,000 companies and 299,000 establishments, of which about 1,700 had more than $500 million in shipments.
- The target is every company with at least $500 million in shipments, plus extra reporters. The panel is about 3,000 companies and about 4,700 reporting units, often divisions of diversified firms.
- Companies reported or imputed cover about **58%** of 2022 manufacturing shipments.
- There are 92 industry categories, combined into 65 published levels.
- **It is not a probability sample.** The method assumes month-to-month change among panel companies represents change for the whole industry.

**Estimation:** Each year, data through March are benchmarked to the Economic Census, the Annual Survey of Manufactures, and the annual Manufacturers' Unfilled Orders Survey. The Annual Integrated Economic Survey is now named as a future benchmark source. Months after the benchmark are carried forward by applying the panel's month-to-month change. The prior month is revised once for late reports, then held until the next benchmark.

**Seasonal adjustment:** X-13ARIMA-SEATS, run each month as new data arrive, with trading-day and month-length adjustments for most shipments series. Seasonally adjusted new orders are calculated from adjusted shipments plus the change in adjusted unfilled orders, not adjusted directly.

**Important quirk:** New and unfilled orders totals **exclude semiconductors**.

**Collection:** online (Census Taker) and fax image capture. Forms are due by about the 10th business day; the advance release uses reports received through about the 18th.

## 6. Releases and access

- **Advance Report on Durable Goods:** about 18 working days after the month ends, 8:30 a.m. ET. It's a major market-moving release.
- **Full Report ("Factory Orders"):** durable and nondurable goods, about a week after the advance report, 10:00 a.m. ET.
- **Benchmark reports:** usually each May (none planned for 2026).
- **Where to get it:**
  - Press releases (PDF): census.gov/m3
  - Time Series/Trend Charts tool and bulk downloads: census.gov/econ/currentdata/?programCode=M3
  - Historical Excel files, NAICS from 1992 and SIC 1958–2001, with documentation (naicshist.pdf) explaining the series codes. Example: `A` + `NXA` + `NO` = seasonally adjusted new orders for nondefense capital goods excluding aircraft.
  - **Census Data API:** `api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/m3` and `/eits/advm3`. An API key is now required.
  - data.gov lists it under a CC0 public-domain license.
  - FRED republishes it (for example DGORDER and NEWORDER; check the IDs yourself).
- **Geography:** national only. There are no state or local figures.

## 7. Who uses it

- **BEA:** inputs to GDP, mainly equipment investment and inventory change. BEA also compiles indicator series from it.
- **Federal Reserve, Treasury, Council of Economic Advisers:** monetary and fiscal policy.
- **The Conference Board:** two of the ten components of the Leading Economic Index come from M3 (new orders for consumer goods and materials, and new orders for nondefense capital goods excluding aircraft). M3 shipments also feed the "manufacturing and trade sales" part of its Coincident Index.
- **Financial markets and the press:** "core capital goods" orders and shipments are a widely watched gauge of business investment.
- **Others:** corporate economists, trade associations, academics, consultants, and Census's own Manufacturing and Trade Inventories and Sales report.

## 8. Benefits to the public

- It is the only federal monthly measure of orders, backlogs, and inventories across all manufacturing. Orders show up before production and hiring do, so it gives early warning of turning points.
- It makes GDP estimates more accurate and timely, and so improves policy decisions.
- It's free and in the public domain, which puts small businesses and the public on the same footing as large firms with private data.
- It runs more than 85 years back (to 1939), which is valuable for research on business cycles.

## 9. Notes for preservationists and data librarians

**Most at risk of being lost:**
- Old press releases
- The methodology PDF (Web_Methodology.pdf), which is updated in place without version history
- SIC-era files and the SIC-to-NAICS crosswalks
- Pre-benchmark versions of the data, since each benchmark overwrites history (keep a snapshot per benchmark)
- The format of API responses

The archive.org scans of Current Industrial Reports cover the 1947–63 revision.

**Recommendations:**
- Save a copy of the data each month the day it's released, because the prior month is always revised.
- Record which benchmark each copy reflects (currently May 2025, 2017 NAICS basis).
- Watch for the change to 2022 NAICS that's coming through the Annual Integrated Economic Survey.

**Points for policy advocates:**
- Participation is voluntary.
- Coverage has slipped: about 64% of shipments in 2012, about 60% in 2017, about 58% in 2022.
- Revisions are frozen in 2026 for lack of resources.
- The 2025 shutdown showed how fragile the data flow is.
- Federal statistical agencies generally face budget and staffing pressure.

## 10. Problems and inconsistencies in Census's documentation

- The "About" page (last reviewed 2019) says "establishments with $500 million or more" and "89 industry categories." The press releases and methodology say *companies*, 92 categories, and a supplemental panel of smaller firms.
- The "About" page says the full report comes about 23 working days after the month. In practice it comes about 5–6 business days after the advance report.
- A 2021 conference paper said seasonal adjustment used X-11. The current methodology says X-13ARIMA-SEATS.
- Panel size has been reported as about 5,000 units and 3,100 companies (2021) and about 4,700 units and 3,000 companies (2025).

**Main sources:**
- census.gov/manufacturing/m3, including the About, Methodology, Benchmark, and historical pages
- Form M-3(SD)
- reginfo.gov records for OMB 0607-0008
- Census Data API documentation
- The 1963 Current Industrial Reports on archive.org
- Conference Board LEI technical notes (2026)
- Shutdown coverage from Reuters and Census

# Risk Assessment: Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories, and Orders (M3)

The ratings come out as three Moderate, one High (staffing and funding) and one No Known Issue (historical data). Nothing I found points to M3 being cut or targeted. The risks come from pressure on the Census Bureau as a whole: lost staff, a cut to its survey budget, leadership changes, and the 2025 shutdown.

Two limits on the research:
- **Staffing tracker:** The tracker page at usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com loads its numbers with JavaScript, so I couldn't read them. It also says it stopped updating on December 31, 2025. The staffing figures below come from the American Statistical Association (ASA) and Congressional Research Service (CRS) instead.
- **Federal Register:** The site blocked automated access. I read the M3 notice through govinfo.gov's copy instead.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence by risk level:**
- **Gone / High:** None found. Historical press releases are still posted, for example the June 2026 report at census.gov/manufacturing/m3/historical_data/pressreleases/prel/2026/jun26prel.pdf. The older SIC-coded files (1958–2001), the NAICS files (1992 onward), the time-series tool and the API (/timeseries/eits/m3 and /advm3) all still work.
- **Moderate:** Each annual benchmark overwrites earlier versions of the history; the most recent one revised seasonally adjusted data back to 2012. This is standard, documented practice, not removal. Census also says historical data "will remain unchanged for the remainder of 2026," which freezes the history rather than deleting it.
- **Context:** The Senate's FY2026 appropriations report asked Census to explain why some Census and BEA datasets were removed (CRS IF12714). None of those concerned M3.

**Rating: No Known Issue.** I found no removed files or variables.

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence by risk level:**
- **High:** None. There is no statutory deadline, no skipped month, and the OMB approval hasn't lapsed.
- **Moderate:** The October 2025 funding lapse delayed scheduled releases. The October 2025 advance report came out December 23, 2025, and the full report on January 7, 2026 (Reuters; Census rescheduling notices).
- **No Known Issue:**
  - The 2026 releases have been on time. The August 2026 full report came out October 2, 2026, and the next release is set for November 3, 2026.
  - OMB approval 0607-0008 is active until March 31, 2027 (reginfo.gov, ICR 202312-0607-002).
  - Census has started renewing it on schedule: a 60-day comment notice for an "extension, without change" appeared on July 20, 2026 (91 FR 45236, FR Doc. 2026-14513; comments closed September 18, 2026).

**Rating: Moderate.** The rubric counts delayed publication as Moderate, and the shutdown delays happened within the past year. The current schedule and renewal process otherwise look healthy.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence by risk level:**
- **High:** The annual benchmark revision and the update of seasonal adjustment models are both skipped for 2026 "due to schedule and resource constraints" (special notice on the M3 page and in every 2026 release). That is a cut in how often the series is updated, and Census says lack of resources is the reason.
- **Moderate:**
  - Seasonal factors and benchmark levels are getting older, so the monthly figures may drift further from the annual survey data they are anchored to.
  - Coverage keeps slipping, from about 64% of manufacturing shipments (2012) to about 60% (2017) to about 58% (2022).
  - Responding is voluntary.
- **No Known Issue / improvement:**
  - Since July 2025, the advance release includes detailed data for all nondurable industries.
  - Monthly frequency and release timing haven't changed.
  - Industry detail hasn't been reduced.

**Rating: Moderate (close to High).** The headline monthly data are unchanged in detail, frequency and timeliness, and in one respect have improved. But the skipped 2026 revision is a resource-driven step back that could become a cut in quality if it continues into 2027.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence by risk level:**
- **High:**
  - The legal authority is named but discretionary. Title 13 §182 lets Census run surveys it considers necessary; §131 covers the economic census.
  - No law requires M3 specifically, and responding is voluntary.
  - Partial alternatives exist, such as the ISM manufacturing survey (PMI) and the Federal Reserve's Industrial Production index.
- **Moderate / No Known Issue:**
  - OMB's own record calls M3 "the only survey that provides monthly statistical information… on the entire manufacturing sector" and "an essential part of the development of the Gross Domestic Product."
  - It is a Principal Federal Economic Indicator under OMB's statistical rules.
  - BEA, the Federal Reserve and The Conference Board's Leading Economic Index (2 of its 10 components) depend on it.
  - The alternatives can't replace it: none gives dollar figures for orders, backlogs and inventories by industry.

**Rating: Moderate.** No law requires M3 by name, but GDP and the national accounts rely on it, and nothing else could substitute for it.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence by risk level:**
- **High:**
  - **Staff:** ASA (*The Nation's Data at Risk 2025*) estimates Census has lost about 15% of its staff since FY2024. Applied to a FY2024 workforce of roughly 8,400 (my estimate, worked back from budget figures), that is about 1,200 people, which passes the rubric's 1,000-staff threshold.
  - **Leadership:** Director Robert Santos left early in 2025. In September 2025 a political appointee, George Cook, replaced the career acting director, Ron Jarmin, who went back to being deputy (NPR, September 19, 2025). Census still has no Senate-confirmed director as of September 2026 (The Federalist, September 4, 2026).
- **Moderate:**
  - The FY2026 budget request proposed cutting the Current Surveys and Programs account (which pays for M3) by about 12%.
  - Congress enacted $318.5M, down about 3% from $329M (P.L. 119-74; CRS IF13105). The Current Economic Statistics line was requested flat at $216M.
  - Rising costs are also eroding what the money buys.
  - Hiring freezes and a backlog of contracts awaiting approval have added strain (ASA; Washington Post).
- **Program-level effect:** The 2026 revision freeze, explicitly blamed on "resource constraints," is the clearest sign of strain specific to M3.

**Rating: High.** This is driven by agency-wide staff losses over 1,000 and the replacement of leadership. The budget cut on its own (about 3%) would not trigger the rating, and I couldn't measure staff losses in the Economic Indicators Division itself.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence by risk level:**
- **High:** None specific to M3. There is no executive-order-driven change to the data collection and no negative policy note on the site. The renewal is "without change."
- **Moderate:**
  - The FY2026 budget proposes reorganizing BLS, BEA and Census within Commerce.
  - The same budget commits to eliminating Census functions "not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission" by the end of FY2026 (Census Project; CRS). Because M3 isn't required by name in law, that language could reach it, though its central role in GDP makes that unlikely.
  - Census has cancelled other surveys (NPR, April 2025), and data has come under wider political pressure, including the widely reported firing of the BLS commissioner in August 2025.
- **No Known Issue:** What M3 collects and publishes hasn't changed since January 2025, apart from the expanded nondurable detail.

**Rating: Moderate.** Proposed restructuring and the "non-mandated functions" directive are pending changes that could affect M3, but nothing targets it directly.

---

## Summary of risk levels
Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue
Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk
Data Quality: Moderate Risk
Statutory Context: Moderate Risk
Staffing and Funding: High Risk
Policy: Moderate Risk

**What to watch next:**
- The release of the September 2026 data (October 27 and November 3)
- OMB's decision on the renewal before March 31, 2027
- Whether the revision freeze continues into 2027
- The FY2027 budget for Current Surveys
- Any plan for reorganizing the statistical agencies or a nomination for Census director
